questions.stem: Per this page, why is `invokeAll()` preferred over the fork-compute-join pattern in a RecursiveAction?

options.text: There is no result to combine, so it is as efficient and reads more cleanly
options.says: The page says RecursiveAction has no result to combine, so computing one subtask inline brings no advantage and invokeAll() is equally efficient and cleaner.

options.text: It runs the subtasks one after the other, so their side effects do not race
options.says: The page says invokeAll() forks all provided tasks and waits for them, and still requires side effects to be thread-safe.

options.text: It skips fork() and join(), so its subtasks start with less scheduling cost
options.says: The page says invokeAll() combines fork() and join() for multiple tasks and handles fork/join internally.

questions.stem: Per this page, why does a counting RecursiveAction tally matches in a plain local int before it touches its AtomicInteger?

options.text: Updating the atomic on each match would lose counts when two leaves add together
options.says: The page offers using AtomicInteger directly as a fix for the counting race; updating it on every iteration costs contention, not counts.

options.text: Far fewer atomic updates are made, so threads contend less over the counter
options.says: The page says one update per base case minimises contention: with K leaf tasks there are only K atomic updates instead of N.

options.text: An AtomicInteger allows one update per task, so each leaf must batch its count
options.says: The page says updating an atomic variable on every iteration causes contention, which means repeated updates are allowed, only slower.
